title: Digital SAT Reading and Writing — Practice Test 8
kicker: American Diploma · Digital SAT · Full practice tests
summary: A full, timed Reading and Writing section in Digital SAT format: two 32-minute modules of 27 questions each, with an explanation for every answer choice and your score by skill.

blocks.text: This is a complete Reading and Writing section in the format of the Digital SAT: **two modules of 27 questions, 32 minutes each (54 questions, 64 minutes)**. Every question has one short passage (or a pair of short passages) and four choices. Inside each module the questions come in the usual order: Craft and Structure, then Information and Ideas, then Standard English Conventions, and Expression of Ideas last. All passages and questions were written for this course.

items: Sit in a quiet place with no phone and about 70 minutes free. Do the whole test in one sitting.
The timer starts when you begin a module. Aim for about 1 minute 11 seconds per question, and do not spend more than 2 minutes on any single question.

Inside a module you can move back and forth between questions. When the 32 minutes end, the module closes. In the real test, you cannot go back to Module 1 once Module 2 starts, so treat this test the same way.
There is no penalty for wrong answers. Never leave a question blank: if time is short, eliminate what you can and guess.
At the end you will see your number correct, your result for each module and each skill, and an explanation for every question.

blocks.title: About your result
blocks.text: The score shown at the end is a practice percentage (the number of questions you answered correctly). It is not an official SAT score. Official Reading and Writing scores are reported on a scale of 200–800, and this page does not convert your result to that scale.

blocks.title: قبل ما تبدأ
blocks.text: اقعد في مكان هادي من غير موبايل، وخلّي معاك حوالي ساعة وربع. الامتحان موديولين، كل واحد 27 سؤال في 32 دقيقة، يعني تقريبًا دقيقة وعشر ثواني للسؤال. جوه الموديول تقدر ترجع لأي سؤال، لكن لما الوقت يخلص الموديول بيقفل، وفي الامتحان الحقيقي مفيش رجوع لـ Module 1. مفيش خصم على الإجابة الغلط، فمتسيبش ولا سؤال فاضي. والنسبة اللي هتظهر في الآخر للتدريب بس، مش درجة SAT رسمية.

blocks.title: Digital SAT Reading and Writing — Practice Test 8
blocks.intro: Two modules, 27 questions each, 32 minutes each. In the real test, 2 questions in each module are unscored pretest items, and Module 2 adapts to your Module 1 performance (it is harder or easier). In this practice test all 54 questions count: Module 1 is a mixed-difficulty module, and Module 2 is the harder version. Once Module 1 ends, you cannot go back to it.

questions.p: While most film composers of his generation filled their scores with full orchestras, Tarek Nassar wrote music that was notably ______: many scenes in his films are accompanied by nothing more than a single cello or a few quiet notes on a piano.
questions.q: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
c: spare
lavish
unpredictable
derivative
questions.e: The contrast with "full orchestras" and the example of a single cello show that Nassar used very few instruments, so "spare" fits. "Lavish" is the trap: it describes the other composers, not Nassar.
ce: Correct: a single cello or a few piano notes is music with very few parts, which is what "spare" means.
Opposite meaning: "lavish" describes the full orchestras of other composers, not Nassar's few instruments.
Nothing in the text says his music surprises listeners; it is about how few instruments he used.
"Derivative" means copied from others, but the text says he did the opposite of most composers.

questions.p: Seismologist Hala Mansour designed her network of low-cost earthquake sensors to ______ the national seismic network rather than to replace it: the inexpensive devices fill the gaps between the existing stations, which remain the main source of data.
questions.q: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
c: undermine
supplement
imitate
postpone
questions.e: The sensors "fill the gaps" while the existing stations "remain the main source of data," so they add to the network: "supplement." "Imitate" fails because the text is about adding coverage, not copying.
ce: "Undermine" means weaken; the sensors help the network instead of harming it.
Correct: filling gaps while the main stations stay in use means adding to the network, which is what "supplement" means.
The sensors fill gaps between stations; the text says nothing about copying how the stations work.
"Postpone" means delay, which makes no sense with a network that is already working.

questions.p:
The following text is from an original story written in the style of an older novel.
The old ferryman had crossed the river twice a day for forty years, and he spoke of it fondly, as one speaks of a ______ neighbour who might shout at you over the fence on Monday and bring you a basket of figs on Tuesday.
questions.q: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
c: temperamental
generous
quiet
absent
questions.e: The neighbour swings from shouting to giving figs, so the river is described as moody and changeable: "temperamental." "Generous" is only half the picture, since it ignores the shouting.
ce: Correct: a neighbour who shouts one day and brings gifts the next has changing moods, which is what "temperamental" means.
Half-right: the basket of figs is generous, but the shouting is not, and the word must cover both.
Contradicted: a neighbour who shouts over the fence is not quiet.
The neighbour appears on both Monday and Tuesday, so "absent" makes no sense.

questions.p: Sociologist Karim Adel found that residents of a newly built apartment district rarely met their neighbours, since the buildings had no shared courtyards or shops. When the district later added a weekly street market, the number of residents who said they knew their neighbours rose sharply. The market, Adel concluded, ______ contact between people who would otherwise have remained strangers.
questions.q: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
c: fostered
prohibited
measured
replaced
questions.e: After the market opened, more residents knew their neighbours, so the market encouraged contact: "fostered." "Measured" fails because the market is the cause of the contact, not a tool for recording it.
ce: Correct: the market helped contact grow, and "fostered" means encouraged or helped to develop.
Opposite meaning: contact increased after the market opened, so it was not forbidden.
The market did not count or record contact; it caused more of it.
Nothing replaced contact; contact itself increased.

questions.p: When people picture global warming, they usually think of rising air temperatures. Yet the air holds only a small share of the extra heat trapped by greenhouse gases; most of it has gone into the oceans. Because water warms slowly and stores heat for a long time, ocean temperatures give scientists a steadier record of the planet's warming than air temperatures, which can swing widely from one year to the next.
questions.q: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
c: To show that the oceans warm more quickly than the air does
To argue that greenhouse gases do not affect air temperatures
To describe the instruments scientists use to measure deep ocean water
To explain why ocean temperatures are a useful measure of how much the planet is warming
questions.e: The text moves from what people usually picture (air) to why the oceans are a better record of warming, so its purpose is to explain the value of ocean temperatures. The "warm more quickly" choice reverses the text, which says water warms slowly.
ce: Reversed: the text says water "warms slowly."
Too extreme and unsupported: the text says the air holds a small share of the heat, not none.
No instruments are described anywhere in the text.
Correct: the text says the oceans hold most of the extra heat and give a "steadier record" than the air.

questions.p:
The following text is from an original story written in the style of an older novel.
The letter lay on the hall table for three days. Mrs. Pell dusted around it each morning, set a vase of fresh roses beside it, and once moved it a little to the left so that the light from the window fell upon the handwriting. __She did not open it.__ Whatever news it carried, she seemed to feel, would keep better sealed.
questions.q: Which choice best describes the function of the underlined sentence in the text as a whole?
c: It explains why the letter was delivered three days late.
It reveals that, despite her careful attention to the letter, the character avoids learning what it says.
It shows that the character is unable to read the handwriting.
It introduces a change in the setting of the story.
questions.e: The details of dusting, roses and light show close attention, and the short underlined sentence reveals the surprise: she never opens it. The handwriting choice fails because the final sentence gives her real reason, a wish not to know the news.
ce: Nothing in the text says the letter was late; it has simply lain on the table.
Correct: after all her care for the letter, the short sentence shows she never reads it, and the next sentence explains why.
She moves the letter into the light to see the handwriting, and her reason is fear of the news, not inability.
The setting stays in the hall; the sentence describes what she does not do.

questions.p:
Text 1
Some music critics argue that streaming services have made listeners less adventurous. Because the services recommend songs similar to those a person already plays, the critics claim, listeners hear an ever narrower range of music.

Text 2
Music researcher Lina Farouk studied the listening records of 10,000 streaming users over five years. The average number of different genres each user played every month rose steadily. Users did follow the services' recommendations, Farouk found, but the recommendations often led them from a familiar style to a related one they had never played before.
questions.q: Based on the texts, how would Farouk (Text 2) most likely respond to the critics' claim in Text 1?
c: She would argue that most users ignore the services' recommendations.
She would agree that recommendations narrow listeners' taste but say this happens slowly.
She would argue that her data contradict the claim, since the users she studied played a wider range of genres over time.
She would say the critics are right about older listeners but wrong about younger ones.
questions.e: The critics predict narrower listening; Farouk measured wider listening, so she would say the evidence goes against them. The "ignore recommendations" choice fails because she reports that users followed them, which is exactly how they found new genres.
ce: Contradicted: she says users "did follow" the recommendations.
Reversed: her data show taste widening, not narrowing slowly.
Correct: Farouk found the number of genres per user rose, the opposite of an "ever narrower range."
Text 2 never divides users by age, so this has no support.

questions.p: In parts of the Arctic, the ground has been frozen for thousands of years. This permafrost contains ice that holds the soil together like cement. As average temperatures rise, the ice in the upper layers melts, and the ground above it can sink unevenly, tilting houses and cracking roads. Engineers in some northern towns now set buildings on posts driven deep into the still-frozen ground, or raise them above the surface so that heat from inside does not reach the soil.
questions.q: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
c: Heat from inside buildings is the main cause of melting permafrost.
Permafrost has been frozen for thousands of years and contains ice.
Many Arctic towns are being abandoned because their roads have cracked.
Melting permafrost can make the ground sink unevenly, so builders in some Arctic towns have changed the way they construct buildings.
questions.e: The text explains a problem caused by warming (sinking ground) and how engineers respond, so the main idea must include both. The "heat from buildings" choice twists a detail: the text names rising temperatures as the cause.
ce: Distorted: rising average temperatures cause the melting; heat from buildings is only something engineers avoid adding.
Too narrow: a true detail from the first lines, not the main idea.
Not supported: the text mentions cracked roads but says nothing about abandoning towns.
Correct: this covers both halves of the text, the problem (sinking ground) and the response (new building methods).

questions.p:
The following text is from an original story written in the style of an older novel.
The orchestra of the little spa town consisted of eleven gentlemen, most of them past sixty, who played every afternoon beneath the striped roof of the bandstand. Their waltzes were somewhat slower than the composer had intended, for the second violin, Mr. Abbot, could no longer manage the quick passages, and the others, out of a kindness they never spoke of, had quietly agreed to keep pace with him.
questions.q: According to the text, why does the orchestra play its waltzes slowly?
c: The composer wrote the waltzes to be played slowly.
The other players slow down so that an older colleague can keep up.
The audience prefers slow music on summer afternoons.
Mr. Abbot, who leads the orchestra, insists on a slow tempo.
questions.e: The text says the players slow down because Mr. Abbot cannot play the quick parts, and they do it out of unspoken kindness. The composer choice reverses the text, which says the tempo is slower than the composer intended.
ce: Reversed: the waltzes are slower "than the composer had intended."
Correct: Mr. Abbot cannot manage the quick passages, and the others agreed "to keep pace with him."
The audience is never mentioned.
Mr. Abbot plays second violin and insists on nothing; the others decide quietly out of kindness.

questions.p: Along one stretch of coast, meadows of seagrass grow in the shallow water just offshore. Marine scientist Nadia Wahba hypothesizes that these meadows protect the beaches behind them, because the dense leaves slow incoming waves before they reach the shore.
questions.q: Which finding, if true, would most directly support Wahba's hypothesis?
c: Storms along this stretch of coast have become more frequent in recent decades.
Seagrass meadows provide shelter for many kinds of young fish.
Over five years, beaches behind seagrass meadows lost much less sand during storms than nearby beaches of similar shape with no seagrass offshore.
Seagrass grows best in clear, shallow water.
questions.e: Wahba's hypothesis is that seagrass protects beaches; only the comparison of beaches with and without seagrass tests that directly, and it shows less sand loss behind the meadows. The fish choice is the tempting off-topic option: it is a benefit of seagrass, but not the one she proposed.
ce: This is about storms, not about whether seagrass reduces their effect on beaches.
True of seagrass in general, perhaps, but it says nothing about protecting beaches.
Correct: comparing similar beaches with and without seagrass shows that the meadows reduce sand loss, which is what Wahba predicts.
This explains where seagrass grows, not what it does for the shore.

questions.p: In an original story written in the style of an older novel, the narrator describes her grandfather's watch-repair shop as a place where time itself seemed to be in no hurry.
questions.q: Which quotation from the story most effectively illustrates this claim?
c: "My grandfather opened the shop each morning at precisely seven o'clock, never a minute late."
"Customers who came in on a moment's errand would find themselves, an hour later, still seated on the bench by the window, listening to the slow chorus of the clocks."
"Outside, the street was full of carts and hurrying clerks."
"He kept his finest tools in a drawer lined with green felt."
questions.e: The claim is about time moving slowly inside the shop, and only the quotation about customers lingering for an hour while the clocks tick slowly shows this. The street quotation describes hurry, but outside the shop, so it does not illustrate the claim.
ce: This shows punctuality, not a place where time is in no hurry.
Correct: a quick errand stretching into an hour, with slow clocks, shows time passing unhurriedly in the shop.
This describes the street outside, not the shop.
A detail about tools with no connection to the pace of time.

questions.p:
Residents who know at least five neighbours by name, by housing type (%)
Housing type | 2014 | 2024
Detached houses | 62 | 55
Low-rise apartments | 48 | 51
High-rise towers | 21 | 34

In 2016, the high-rise towers in one city opened shared rooftop gardens where residents could grow vegetables together. A survey suggests that the gardens may have helped neighbours get to know one another: ______
questions.q: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to complete the statement?
c: in high-rise towers, the share of residents who knew at least five neighbours by name rose from 21% in 2014 to 34% in 2024.
in detached houses, the share of residents who knew at least five neighbours by name fell from 62% to 55%.
in low-rise apartments, the share rose from 48% to 51%.
in 2024, residents of high-rise towers were more likely than residents of any other housing type to know five neighbours by name.
questions.e: The claim is about the towers, where the gardens opened, so the data must show the towers' rise from 21% to 34%. The "more likely than any other type" choice misreads the table: the towers were still the lowest in 2024.
ce: Correct: the gardens were added to the towers, and this choice shows the towers' share rising after they opened.
True, but detached houses did not get the rooftop gardens, so this does not support the claim.
True, but low-rise apartments are not the buildings with the gardens.
False: in 2024 the towers (34%) were still lowest, below low-rise apartments (51%) and houses (55%).

questions.p:
Average date of the first autumn frost in Tavor Valley, by decade
Decade | Average date
1980s | October 2
1990s | October 6
2000s | October 11
2010s | October 15

A team of climatologists studying Tavor Valley found that the growing season there, which ends with the first autumn frost, has lengthened in recent decades. Their records show that ______
questions.q: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to complete the statement?
c: the average date of the first autumn frost moved from October 2 in the 1980s to October 15 in the 2010s.
the first autumn frost has arrived in October, on average, in every decade since the 1980s.
the first autumn frost arrived earlier in each decade than in the decade before.
the average date of the first autumn frost in the 2000s was October 6.
questions.e: The growing season ends with the first frost, so a later frost means a longer season; the October 2 → October 15 change shows this. The "in October every decade" choice is true but shows no change at all.
ce: Correct: a frost that comes later each decade means the growing season ends later, so it is longer.
True, but it does not show any change, so it cannot show that the season has lengthened.
False: the dates get later each decade, not earlier.
False: October 6 is the 1990s figure; the 2000s figure is October 11.

questions.p: Engineers testing a new type of road surface found that it soaked up rainwater far better than ordinary asphalt, leaving fewer puddles after storms. During winter tests, however, water trapped inside the new surface froze and expanded, opening small cracks that grew larger each time the water thawed and froze again. The engineers therefore concluded that the new surface ______
questions.q: Which choice most logically completes the text?
c: absorbs less rainwater than ordinary asphalt does.
should replace ordinary asphalt on every road as soon as possible.
may be better suited to places with mild winters than to places where temperatures often fall below freezing.
does not crack when the water inside it freezes.
questions.e: The surface has one strength (rain) and one weakness (freezing), so the logical conclusion is that it fits places where freezing is rare. Replacing asphalt everywhere ignores the winter cracking the engineers found.
ce: Contradicted: it soaked up rainwater "far better" than asphalt.
Too extreme: the cracking problem in winter argues against using it everywhere.
Correct: it works well with rain but cracks when trapped water freezes, so it suits places without frequent freezing.
Contradicted: freezing water opened cracks in the surface.

questions.p: Icebergs are made of fresh water even though they float in the salty ______ they break off from glaciers, which form on land from snow that has been pressed into ice over many years.
questions.q: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
c: sea, which
sea,
sea
sea;
questions.e: "Icebergs are made of fresh water even though they float in the salty sea" and "they break off from glaciers…" are both complete sentences, so a semicolon is needed. A comma alone makes a comma splice.
ce: "Which they break off from glaciers" is not a correct clause, so the sentence becomes ungrammatical.
Comma splice: a comma alone cannot join two complete sentences.
Run-on: the two complete sentences are fused with no punctuation.
Correct: both parts are complete sentences, and a semicolon joins two complete sentences.

questions.p: Sayed Darwish, a composer from Alexandria who wrote many of Egypt's best-loved songs in the early twentieth ______ died in 1923 at the age of thirty-one.
questions.q: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
c: century
century,
century;
century—
questions.e: The phrase "a composer from Alexandria… century" is extra information about Darwish that opens with a comma, so it must close with a comma. The dash fails because a comma and a dash do not make a matching pair.
ce: The extra information opened with a comma, so it must close with one before the verb "died."
Correct: the comma closes the extra information that began with the comma after "Darwish," so the pair matches.
A semicolon would cut the subject "Sayed Darwish" off from its verb "died."
A dash cannot close extra information that was opened with a comma; the pair must match.

questions.p: Much of what we know about the deep interior of our planet comes from studying earthquake waves. Geologists usually divide the inside of Earth into three main ______ the crust, the mantle, and the core.
questions.q: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
c: layers:
layers;
layers, such as:
layers
questions.e: The words before the blank form a complete sentence, and what follows is a list of the three layers, so a colon is correct. The semicolon fails because the list is not a complete sentence.
ce: Correct: a complete sentence comes before the list, so a colon can introduce it.
A semicolon must join two complete sentences, and "the crust, the mantle, and the core" is only a list.
A colon should not follow "such as"; and "such as" wrongly suggests the three named layers are only examples.
With no punctuation, the list runs straight into "layers" and the sentence does not read correctly.

questions.p: The narrow alleys that wind through the old quarter of one Mediterranean ______ stay cool even in August, since the tall walls on either side shade the ground for most of the day.
questions.q: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
c: port—
port,
port;
port
questions.e: The long subject ends at "port" and the verb "stay" follows, so no punctuation is needed. A comma is the tempting trap because the subject is long, but a comma must never separate a subject from its verb.
ce: A single dash would wrongly split the subject from its verb.
A single comma would separate the subject "alleys" from its verb "stay."
A semicolon needs complete sentences on both sides; "The narrow alleys … port" has no verb.
Correct: "The narrow alleys … port" is the subject and "stay" is its verb, and no punctuation goes between a subject and its verb.

questions.p: Each of the electric buses in the city's new fleet ______ a battery that can be fully recharged overnight at the depot, so the buses can run all day without stopping to charge.
questions.q: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
c: are carrying
carry
carries
have carried
questions.e: The subject is "Each" (singular), not "buses," so the verb must be "carries." "Carry" is the trap: it agrees with the nearest noun instead of the subject.
ce: Plural verb: "Each" is singular.
Plural verb: it agrees with "buses," which is inside the phrase "of the electric buses," not the subject.
Correct: the subject is "Each," which is singular, so it takes the singular verb "carries."
Plural verb, and the past form does not fit a description of how the fleet works now.

questions.p: In 1958, Egyptian director Youssef Chahine ______ Cairo Station, a film in which he also played one of the leading roles. The film is set almost entirely in and around the city's main railway station.
questions.q: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
c: released
releases
has released
will release
questions.e: A specific past date calls for the simple past, "released." "Has released" is the strongest trap, but the present perfect is not used with a finished time like "In 1958."
ce: Correct: "In 1958" names a finished time in the past, so the simple past is needed.
Present tense does not fit an action dated 1958.
The present perfect cannot be used with a finished past time such as "In 1958."
Future tense contradicts the date in the past.

questions.p: In one limestone region, geologists are still exploring a vast cave system. Formed over millions of years by slightly acidic water slowly dissolving the rock, ______
questions.q: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
c: more than twenty kilometers have been mapped by geologists in the cave.
geologists have so far mapped more than twenty kilometers of the cave's passages.
the mapping of the cave's passages now covers more than twenty kilometers.
the cave's passages now stretch for more than twenty kilometers.
questions.e: The opening phrase describes something formed by water dissolving rock, so the subject right after the comma must be the cave's passages. The "geologists" choice is the trap: it sounds natural but says the geologists were formed by water.
ce: Dangling modifier: "twenty kilometers" is a distance that was mapped, not something formed by water.
Dangling modifier: this says the geologists were formed by acidic water.
Dangling modifier: the mapping was not formed by water dissolving rock.
Correct: the passages are what water formed, so they must come right after the opening phrase.

questions.p: The deep-sea floor receives no sunlight at all, so no plants can grow there. ______ whole communities of tubeworms, clams, and shrimp thrive around hydrothermal vents on the sea floor, fed by bacteria that draw energy from chemicals in the hot vent water.
questions.q: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
c: Nevertheless,
Consequently,
For instance,
Similarly,
questions.e: The first sentence suggests the sea floor should be lifeless; the second says life thrives there anyway, so a contrast is needed: "Nevertheless." "Consequently" fails because darkness is not the cause of the thriving communities.
ce: Correct: life thriving where no plants can grow is surprising given the first sentence, so a contrast transition fits.
Cause-effect is wrong: a lack of sunlight does not cause communities to thrive.
The vent communities are not an example of a place without plants growing; they are a surprising exception.
The second sentence does not describe something similar; it goes against what the first sentence leads us to expect.

questions.p: The first version of a solar-powered water pump built by engineer Omar Fikry worked well on sunny days but stopped completely whenever clouds passed overhead. ______ Fikry added a small battery that stores extra energy during bright periods and releases it when the sunlight weakens.
questions.q: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
c: In other words,
To address this weakness,
Likewise,
By contrast,
questions.e: The first sentence names a problem and the second describes a fix, so the transition must signal a solution: "To address this weakness." "In other words" fails because nothing is being restated.
ce: The second sentence does not restate the first; it describes a new step.
Correct: the battery is Fikry's solution to the problem described in the first sentence.
Adding a battery is not similar to the pump stopping; it is a response to it.
The battery is not set against the problem as a contrast; it is a fix for it.

questions.p: In many cities, retired people who live alone say they often feel lonely, while university students struggle to find housing they can afford. A program in one city addresses both problems by pairing retirees who have spare rooms with students. The students pay a low rent; ______ they agree to share meals with their hosts several times a week.
questions.q: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
c: for example,
nevertheless,
in return,
similarly,
questions.e: The two parts describe an exchange: the students get cheap rent and give company in return. "Nevertheless" fails because there is no contrast between the two actions.
ce: Sharing meals is not an example of paying low rent.
Nothing in paying low rent makes sharing meals surprising, so a contrast is illogical.
Correct: sharing meals is what the students give back for the low rent, an exchange.
Sharing meals is not similar to paying rent; it is the second half of an exchange.

questions.p:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• Inge Lehmann was a Danish seismologist.
• Seismologists study earthquakes and the waves they send through Earth.
• Lehmann studied records of earthquake waves that had passed through Earth's interior.
• Some waves appeared in places where scientists at the time did not expect them.
• In 1936, she published her explanation: Earth has an inner core, inside the outer core.
questions.q: The student wants to present Lehmann and her discovery to an audience unfamiliar with her. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
c: Lehmann noticed that some waves appeared in places where they were not expected.
In 1936, it was proposed that Earth has an inner core inside the outer core.
Seismologists study earthquakes and the waves they send through Earth.
Danish seismologist Inge Lehmann, who studied records of earthquake waves passing through Earth, published evidence in 1936 that the planet has an inner core.
questions.e: The audience does not know Lehmann, so the sentence must say who she was and what she found; only one choice does both. The "In 1936, it was proposed" choice states the discovery but leaves Lehmann out completely.
ce: It gives a detail but does not introduce who she was or state the discovery.
It states the discovery but never introduces Lehmann at all.
General background only; it says nothing about Lehmann or her discovery.
Correct: it introduces who Lehmann was, explains briefly what she studied, and states her discovery.

questions.p:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• The theremin is an electronic musical instrument.
• It was invented in Russia in about 1920 by Leon Theremin.
• It is played without being touched.
• The player moves their hands near two metal antennas.
• One antenna controls the pitch (how high or low the note is), and the other controls the volume.
• Its eerie sound has been used in many film soundtracks.
questions.q: The student wants to explain how the theremin is played. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
c: Invented in Russia in about 1920, the theremin has been heard in many film soundtracks.
A theremin is played without being touched: the player moves their hands near two antennas, one controlling the pitch and the other the volume.
The theremin, an electronic instrument invented by Leon Theremin, has an eerie sound.
Leon Theremin invented the theremin in Russia in about 1920.
questions.e: The goal is to explain how the theremin is played, so the answer must describe the hands and antennas. The soundtrack choice is accurate but answers a different question (where the instrument has been used).
ce: It gives history and use but does not explain how the instrument is played.
Correct: it explains exactly how the instrument is played, using the notes about the hands and the two antennas.
It describes the sound, not the way the player produces it.
Only the inventor and date; nothing about playing it.

questions.p:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• Sociologist Mariam Tawfik studied two neighbourhoods in the same city.
• In Neighbourhood A, small shops occupy the ground floors of the apartment buildings.
• Neighbourhood B has only apartment buildings; its residents shop at a mall three kilometers away.
• Residents of Neighbourhood A reported an average of 14 conversations with neighbours a week.
• Residents of Neighbourhood B reported an average of 4.
questions.q: The student wants to emphasize a difference between the two neighbourhoods. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
c: Sociologist Mariam Tawfik studied two neighbourhoods in the same city.
Residents of the neighbourhood with ground-floor shops reported an average of 14 conversations with neighbours a week, whereas residents of the neighbourhood without shops reported just 4.
In one neighbourhood Tawfik studied, small shops occupy the ground floors of the apartment buildings.
Residents of one neighbourhood shop at a mall three kilometers away.
questions.e: To emphasize a difference, the sentence must compare both neighbourhoods; only one choice gives both figures (14 and 4). The other choices each describe a single neighbourhood or the study in general.
ce: It introduces the study but states no difference.
Correct: it states the difference between the two neighbourhoods, with both figures and the feature that separates them.
It describes only one neighbourhood, so no difference is shown.
Again only one neighbourhood; there is no comparison.

questions.p: Critics who dismiss the film scores of composer Leila Haddad as mere decoration overlook how ______ the music is to the films' storytelling: in several of her films, a melody first heard in a joyful scene returns later, slightly altered, to signal that a character's hopes have been disappointed.
questions.q: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
c: opposed
incidental
integral
superior
questions.e: The example shows the music carrying meaning in the story, so the critics overlook how essential it is: "integral." "Incidental" is the trap, because it matches the critics' "mere decoration" view that the text rejects.
ce: The music works with the storytelling, not against it.
"Incidental" means minor or not essential, which is the critics' view the text argues against.
Correct: a melody that returns to tell the audience something about a character is an essential part of the story, which is what "integral" means.
The text does not rank the music above the storytelling; it says the music is part of it.

questions.p: When a geologist first argued that the region's deep canyon had been carved by a single enormous flood rather than by slow erosion over millions of years, her claim was met with ______: most of her colleagues considered the evidence far too thin to support such a dramatic conclusion.
questions.q: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
c: skepticism
enthusiasm
indifference
confusion
questions.e: The colon explains the reaction: colleagues found the evidence too thin, so they doubted the claim: "skepticism." "Indifference" fails because the colleagues actively judged the evidence instead of ignoring it.
ce: Correct: thinking the evidence is "far too thin" means doubting the claim, which is skepticism.
Opposite: colleagues who think the evidence is too thin are not enthusiastic.
The colleagues judged the evidence and rejected it, so they cared about the claim; they were doubtful, not uninterested.
The colleagues understood the claim; they simply did not believe the evidence supported it.

questions.p:
The following text is from an original story written in the style of an older novel.
Her aunt's kindness was of a peculiar, ______ sort: she would walk two miles through the rain to bring a sick neighbour a pot of soup, and then spend the whole visit listing the ways in which the neighbour had brought the illness upon herself.
questions.q: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
c: tender
prickly
secret
effortless
questions.e: The aunt does a kind deed and then criticizes the person she helps, so her kindness is real but sharp: "prickly." "Tender" is half-right, since it fits the soup but not the scolding.
ce: Listing the neighbour's faults is not tender, so the word ignores half the description.
Correct: the kindness is real (the soup) but hard to receive (the criticism), and "prickly" captures that difficult, sharp quality.
Walking to a neighbour's house with soup is not done in secret.
Walking two miles through the rain takes effort.

questions.p: Engineers once regarded the swaying of tall buildings in strong winds as a problem to be ______ altogether by making structures as stiff as possible. Many modern skyscrapers instead accept some movement and use heavy weights hung near their tops to reduce it.
questions.q: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
c: eliminated
tolerated
measured
celebrated
questions.e: The word "instead" contrasts the old view with modern buildings that "accept some movement," so the old view tried to remove movement completely: "eliminated." "Tolerated" is the trap because it describes the modern approach, not the old one.
ce: Correct: making buildings as stiff as possible was an attempt to remove the swaying "altogether," which is what "eliminated" means.
Accepting some movement is what modern buildings do; the earlier approach tried to stop it, so this reverses the contrast.
Stiffening a building does not measure swaying, and "measured altogether" makes little sense.
No one in the text celebrates the swaying; it is a problem.

questions.p: The survey that sociologist Hossam Nabil gave to shopkeepers in the old market was deliberately ______: rather than asking about prices, profits, or customers, it explored only how the shopkeepers' relationships with one another had changed since a large mall opened nearby.
questions.q: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
c: hasty
exhaustive
narrow
anonymous
questions.e: The colon explains the blank: the survey left out several topics and covered "only" one, so it was deliberately narrow. "Exhaustive" is the opposite of what the text describes.
ce: Nothing in the text suggests the survey was rushed.
"Exhaustive" means covering everything, the opposite of a survey that leaves out prices, profits and customers.
Correct: a survey that explores "only" one topic and skips others on purpose has a narrow focus.
The colon explains what the survey covered, not whether names were recorded.

questions.p: For centuries, sailors told stories of huge, steep waves that rose without warning from moderate seas. Many scientists treated these accounts as exaggerations, since standard models of the ocean predicted that such waves should almost never occur. Then, on January 1, 1995, instruments on the Draupner gas platform in the North Sea recorded a single wave about 26 meters high, far taller than the waves around it. The measurement led researchers to revise their models, and later studies suggested that such "rogue waves" are less rare than was once believed.
questions.q: Which choice best describes the overall structure of the text?
c: It compares two models of the ocean and argues that one of them is more accurate.
It explains how rogue waves form and then suggests ways to protect ships from them.
It describes accounts that experts doubted, presents a measurement that supported those accounts, and notes how scientific views changed as a result.
It presents a measurement and then explains why scientists rejected it.
questions.e: The text moves from doubted sailors' stories to a measurement that confirmed them and then to revised scientific views. The last-step trap reverses the outcome: scientists accepted the measurement and changed their models.
ce: Only "standard models" are mentioned, and no two models are compared.
The text never explains how the waves form or how to protect ships.
Correct: doubted stories → the 1995 measurement → revised models, in that order.
Reversed: the measurement led scientists to change their models, not to reject the measurement.

questions.p: Many listeners assume that the slow tempo of a lullaby is what soothes a crying infant. __In a study by psychologist Rana Elsayed, however, infants calmed just as quickly when lullabies were played at a moderate tempo, as long as the song was sung by a familiar voice.__ Elsayed suggests that who sings may matter more than how fast the song is sung.
questions.q: Which choice best describes the function of the underlined sentence in the text as a whole?
c: It explains why most lullabies are written at a slow tempo.
It offers evidence that supports the common assumption described in the first sentence.
It describes in detail the method Elsayed used to select the infants in her study.
It presents a finding that challenges a common assumption about why lullabies soothe infants.
questions.e: The underlined sentence reports a result that contradicts the belief that slow tempo is what soothes infants, setting up Elsayed's alternative idea. The "supports the assumption" choice is the reversal trap.
ce: It does not explain why lullabies are slow; it questions whether slowness is what matters.
Reversed: "however" signals that the finding goes against the assumption.
The sentence reports a result; it gives no detail about how infants were chosen.
Correct: the study shows tempo did not matter as long as the voice was familiar, which goes against the assumption in the first sentence.

questions.p:
Text 1
Some researchers have proposed adding small amounts of iron to areas of the ocean where the growth of plankton is limited by a lack of iron. The iron would trigger huge blooms of plankton, which absorb carbon dioxide as they grow. When the plankton died and sank, the carbon they contained would be stored in the deep ocean for centuries.

Text 2
Oceanographer Selim Hafez agrees that adding iron can produce large plankton blooms; experiments at sea have shown this clearly. But he points out that in several of those experiments, most of the plankton were eaten or broke down near the surface, returning much of their carbon to the water and the air instead of carrying it to the deep ocean.
questions.q: Based on the texts, how would Hafez (Text 2) most likely respond to the proposal described in Text 1?
c: He would argue that larger amounts of iron should be added to make the method work.
He would reject the idea that iron can trigger plankton blooms.
He would accept that adding iron can increase plankton growth but question whether much of the absorbed carbon would actually reach the deep ocean.
He would claim that plankton do not absorb carbon dioxide as they grow.
questions.e: Hafez accepts the first step of the proposal (blooms) but doubts the last step (long-term storage in the deep ocean). The "reject blooms" choice is the trap: he explicitly agrees with that part.
ce: He never suggests adding more iron; his concern is where the carbon ends up.
Contradicted: he says experiments "have shown this clearly."
Correct: Hafez agrees about the blooms but says the carbon often returns to the water and air near the surface.
He does not dispute that plankton absorb carbon; he questions whether it stays stored.

questions.p:
The following text is from an original story written in the style of an older novel.
For thirty years Mr. Crane had kept the lighthouse on the point, and in all that time he had never once wished to leave it. When the company wrote to say that from the spring the light would be worked by machinery, and that his services would no longer be required, he read the letter at the window, folded it with great care, and climbed the winding stair to polish the great lens, as he did every evening, though there was now no one to see that he did it.
questions.q: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
c: A lighthouse keeper is relieved to learn that he will finally be able to leave the point.
A lighthouse keeper angrily refuses to accept the company's decision.
A long-serving lighthouse keeper quietly continues his duties even after learning that his job will soon end.
A lighthouse keeper explains how the new machinery will work the light.
questions.e: The key detail is that Crane goes on polishing the lens though no one will see, which shows quiet devotion despite losing his post. The "relieved" choice contradicts the statement that he never wished to leave.
ce: Contradicted: he "had never once wished to leave it."
Not supported: he folds the letter "with great care" and shows no anger.
Correct: after reading the letter, he climbs up and polishes the lens as usual, showing calm devotion to his work.
He explains nothing; the machinery is mentioned only in the letter.

questions.p: In one hilly region, small earthquakes are common, but most are too weak to be felt. Seismologist Farida Nour hypothesizes that many of these small earthquakes are triggered by heavy seasonal rain: as rainwater soaks deep into the ground, it raises the water pressure inside cracks in the rock, making it easier for the rock to slip.
questions.q: Which finding, if true, would most directly support Nour's hypothesis?
c: A nearby dry region with similar rock has just as many small earthquakes each year.
The region receives more rain each year than most other parts of the country.
Most of the small earthquakes in the region begin less than five kilometers below the surface.
Over ten years, small earthquakes in the region were most frequent in the weeks just after the rainiest months and were rare during the dry season.
questions.e: If rain triggers earthquakes, earthquakes should cluster after the wet season, and that is what the correct finding shows. The dry-region finding is the reversal trap: it suggests rain makes no difference.
ce: This would weaken the hypothesis, since earthquakes would be just as common without rain.
It shows the region is rainy but not that rain is linked to the timing of earthquakes.
Depth alone does not connect the earthquakes to rainfall.
Correct: earthquakes following the rain, with a short delay for water to soak in, is the pattern Nour's hypothesis predicts.

questions.p: Engineer Dalia Morsi notes that the number of pothole repairs needed on one city's main road fell sharply after 2020, the year the road was resurfaced with a new asphalt mix. She claims that the new mix caused the drop.
questions.q: Which finding, if true, would most directly weaken Morsi's claim?
c: The new asphalt mix costs more per kilometer than the old one.
Repairs fell by the same amount after 2020 on nearby roads that were not resurfaced, after the city banned heavy trucks from the whole district that year.
The main road carries more traffic than any other road in the city.
Potholes in the city form most often in the rainy winter months.
questions.e: To weaken a cause-effect claim, show that the effect happened without the cause: roads without the new mix improved just as much, and a truck ban offers another explanation. Cost and traffic details do not touch the claim.
ce: Cost has nothing to do with whether the mix reduced potholes.
Correct: if roads without the new mix improved just as much, something else (the truck ban) is a likelier cause, which weakens Morsi's claim.
This does not explain the drop in repairs, so it does not test her claim.
Seasonal timing does not explain why repairs fell after 2020.

questions.p:
Average daily listening time of residents in one city, by format (minutes)
Format | 2016 | 2024
Radio | 52 | 38
Streaming services | 31 | 74
CDs and records | 18 | 9

A music researcher surveyed residents of one city in 2016 and 2024 and concluded that, during this period, streaming services replaced radio as the residents' main way of listening to music.
questions.q: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to support the researcher's conclusion?
c: Daily listening time on CDs and records fell by half between 2016 and 2024.
Daily listening time on streaming services more than doubled, from 31 minutes in 2016 to 74 minutes in 2024.
Daily listening time on the radio fell from 52 minutes in 2016 to 38 minutes in 2024.
In 2016, residents listened to the radio for 52 minutes a day and to streaming services for 31, but by 2024 they listened to streaming services for 74 minutes and to the radio for 38.
questions.e: "Replaced radio as the main way" needs a comparison in both years: radio first in 2016, streaming first in 2024. The "more than doubled" choice is true but half-right, because it does not compare streaming with radio.
ce: True, but CDs and records are not part of the conclusion.
True, but it never compares streaming with radio, so it cannot show that streaming took radio's place.
True, but it says nothing about streaming overtaking radio.
Correct: it shows radio ahead in 2016 and streaming ahead in 2024, which is exactly what "replaced radio as the main way" means.

questions.p:
Ice cover on four lakes in one northern region
Lake | Average depth (m) | Ice-cover days per winter, 1980s | Ice-cover days per winter, 2010s
Kesten | 4 | 112 | 101
Morra | 6 | 105 | 93
Lune | 22 | 96 | 70
Tarvo | 31 | 90 | 61

Comparing records from the 1980s and the 2010s, a team of researchers concluded that deeper lakes in the region have lost more days of ice cover each winter than shallow lakes have.
questions.q: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to support the researchers' conclusion?
c: Lake Tarvo, with an average depth of 31 meters, lost 29 days of ice cover per winter, whereas Lake Kesten, with an average depth of 4 meters, lost only 11.
Lake Kesten had more days of ice cover than Lake Tarvo in both the 1980s and the 2010s.
Lake Lune had 70 days of ice cover per winter in the 2010s, fewer than it had in the 1980s.
Lake Morra, with an average depth of 6 meters, lost more days of ice cover than Lake Lune did.
questions.e: The conclusion links depth to the amount of ice lost, so the answer must compare a deep and a shallow lake's losses: Tarvo lost 29 days, Kesten 11. The Kesten-vs-Tarvo ice days choice is true but compares totals, not losses.
ce: Correct: it compares a deep lake with a shallow one and shows the deep lake losing far more days (29 vs 11).
True, but it compares the number of ice days, not how many days each lake lost.
True, but it describes only one lake, so it shows no link between depth and loss.
False: Morra lost 12 days (105 to 93) and Lune lost 26 (96 to 70).

questions.p: In a study of one city's public libraries, a team of sociologists found that branches that began staying open until 9 p.m. saw a large rise in visits by teenagers, while visits by other age groups barely changed. In interviews, many teenagers said that before the change, the branches near them had closed shortly after the end of the school day. The team's findings suggest that ______
questions.q: Which choice most logically completes the text?
c: early closing times, rather than a lack of interest, had kept many teenagers from using the libraries.
teenagers prefer libraries to every other public place in the city.
the longer opening hours caused many adults to stop visiting the libraries.
libraries could save money by closing earlier without losing any visitors.
questions.e: Teenagers came once the libraries stayed open later and said the earlier hours had been the problem, so the barrier was time, not interest. The "adults stopped visiting" choice contradicts the finding that other groups barely changed.
ce: Correct: teenagers came in large numbers once the hours allowed it, so time, not interest, had been the barrier.
Too extreme: no other public places are compared.
Contradicted: visits by other age groups "barely changed."
Contradicted: later hours brought in many more teenage visitors.

questions.p: In the far North Atlantic, surface water that has become cold and salty grows dense enough to sink toward the ocean floor, and this sinking helps drive a vast system of currents that carries heat around the globe. Fresh water is less dense than salt water. Because melting ice from Greenland adds large amounts of fresh water to this part of the ocean, some scientists worry that the meltwater could ______
questions.q: Which choice most logically completes the text?
c: make the surface water sink faster toward the ocean floor.
make the surface water there saltier and so speed up the currents.
make the surface water there less dense and so weaken the sinking that helps drive the currents.
stop the surface water from cooling during the winter.
questions.e: Sinking depends on dense water, and fresh water is less dense, so meltwater could weaken the sinking and the currents. The "sink faster" choice reverses the chain of cause and effect.
ce: Reversed: lighter, fresher water sinks less, not faster.
Reversed: adding fresh water makes seawater less salty, not saltier.
Correct: fresh water lowers density, and less dense water sinks less, so the current system could weaken.
Nothing in the text links fresh water to whether the water cools.

questions.p: The festival screened three restored films: a silent comedy from 1925, filmed in ______ a musical from 1951, made in Cairo; and a war drama from 1962, shot in Belgrade.
questions.q: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
c: Paris:
Paris,
Paris
Paris;
questions.e: Each film in the list contains a comma, so the items are separated by semicolons, as after "Cairo." A comma is the trap: it would blur where one item ends and the next begins.
ce: A colon already introduces the list, and a second colon cannot separate list items.
With only a comma, the reader cannot tell where the first film ends, and it does not match the semicolon after "Cairo."
No punctuation runs the first and second films together.
Correct: the list items already contain commas, so semicolons separate them (the SAT/ACT extra rule), matching the semicolon after "Cairo."

questions.p: Mary Shelley began writing Frankenstein during a stormy summer near Lake Geneva in 1816. The novel's first edition—published in three volumes in ______ did not carry her name on its title page.
questions.q: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
questions.e: "Published in three volumes in 1818" is extra information opened with a dash, so it must close with a dash. The comma fails because dash…comma is not a matching pair.
ce: Without a closing dash, the extra information runs into the verb "did not carry."
A comma cannot close information that was opened with a dash; the pair must match.
Correct: the extra information opened with a dash after "edition," so it must close with a dash.
A semicolon would cut the subject "The novel's first edition" off from its verb.

questions.p: Engineers tested the new steel cables on the bridge for six months. Their tests showed that, even under the heaviest ______ the cables stretched less than the designers had predicted.
questions.q: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
c: loads
loads,
loads;
loads—
questions.e: "Even under the heaviest loads" is an interrupting phrase set off by a pair of commas, so a comma is needed after "loads." The dash fails because the pair must match.
ce: The phrase opened with a comma, so it needs a closing comma before the clause continues.
Correct: the comma closes the phrase "even under the heaviest loads," which opened with a comma after "that."
A semicolon needs complete sentences on both sides; "Their tests showed that, even under the heaviest loads" is not one.
A dash cannot close a phrase that opened with a comma.

questions.p: Sociologists use the term "gentrification" to describe a familiar pattern in ______ wealthier residents move into a lower-income area, rents and property prices rise, and many long-time residents can no longer afford to stay.
questions.q: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
c: cities, such as
cities,
cities
cities:
questions.e: The first part is a complete sentence and the second part explains what the pattern is, so a colon is correct. A comma alone would create a comma splice.
ce: "Such as wealthier residents move…" is ungrammatical, because "such as" must be followed by a noun, not a full clause.
Comma splice: "wealthier residents move…" is a complete sentence and cannot be joined with a comma alone.
Run-on: two complete sentences run together with no punctuation.
Correct: a complete sentence comes before, and what follows explains the pattern, so a colon fits.

questions.p: A traditional Egyptian takht is a small ensemble of musicians. Among the instruments usually heard in a takht ______ the qanun, a zither with dozens of strings that the player plucks with small picks worn on the fingers.
questions.q: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
c: have been
are
is
were
questions.e: In this inverted sentence the subject comes after the verb: "the qanun" is singular, so "is." "Are" is the trap, because "instruments" comes right before the blank but is not the subject.
ce: Plural verb, and it does not match the present-tense description.
Plural verb: it agrees with "instruments," which is inside the introductory phrase, not the subject.
Correct: the sentence is inverted, and the real subject is "the qanun" (singular), so the verb is "is."
Plural and past; the subject "the qanun" is singular and the text is in the present.

questions.p: In 1843, mathematician Ada Lovelace published long notes on Charles Babbage's planned calculating machine, the Analytical Engine, ______ a step-by-step method by which the machine could calculate a series of numbers known as Bernoulli numbers.
questions.q: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
c: she described
describing
describes
to have described
questions.e: The sentence already has a main verb ("published"), so the added phrase needs a non-finite form: "describing." "She described" creates a comma splice.
ce: Comma splice: "she described…" is a complete sentence joined to the first with only a comma.
Correct: the participle "describing" adds information about the notes without creating a second main clause.
A second finite verb with no subject or conjunction makes the sentence ungrammatical, and the present tense clashes with "1843."
The infinitive does not attach logically to the sentence; it reads as if her purpose was to have described the method.

questions.p: Many of the city's oldest markets have been demolished or rebuilt in recent decades, but the fish market near the harbour still stands in ______ original nineteenth-century hall.
questions.q: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
c: they're
their
it's
its
questions.e: The hall belongs to the fish market (singular), so the possessive "its" is needed. "Their" is tempting because "markets" appears earlier, but those markets are not the ones standing in the hall.
ce: "They're" means "they are," which makes no sense here.
Plural: "their" would point to the other markets, but the hall belongs to the fish market.
"It's" means "it is," which makes no sense before "original hall."
Correct: the possessive pronoun refers to the singular "the fish market."

questions.p: The glaciers in one mountain region have lost about a third of their ice since 1980. In the short term, this melting has increased the amount of water flowing into the region's rivers each summer. ______ as the glaciers keep shrinking, scientists expect summer river flow to decline, since less and less ice will remain to melt.
questions.q: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
c: Eventually, though,
As a result,
Similarly,
In other words,
questions.e: The text contrasts more water now with less water later, so the transition must signal both a later time and a contrast: "Eventually, though." "As a result" fails because the future decline is not caused by the present increase.
ce: Correct: the sentence turns from the short-term increase to a long-term decline, so a contrast in time is needed.
The decline is not a result of the increase; it is the opposite trend later on.
A decline is not similar to an increase.
The third sentence does not restate the second; it predicts the opposite.

questions.p: Most early recordings captured sound acoustically: musicians played into a large horn, which channeled the sound to a needle that cut grooves into a disc. Quiet instruments were often barely audible in these recordings. ______ once electrical recording with microphones became common in the mid-1920s, studios could capture far softer sounds.
questions.q: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
c: For example,
By contrast,
Likewise,
That is,
questions.e: The acoustic method lost quiet sounds, and the electrical method captured them, so the sentences contrast: "By contrast." "Likewise" fails because the two methods differ.
ce: Electrical recording is not an example of quiet instruments being lost; it is a different method.
Correct: electrical recording could capture soft sounds, which is the opposite of the acoustic method's weakness.
The new method is not similar to the old one; it fixed its weakness.
The last sentence does not restate the previous one; it describes a change.

questions.p:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• Sociologist Amr Lotfy studied how residents of one district use a newly opened public park.
• He observed the park for 120 hours over six months.
• During each visit, he recorded who used the park, at what time, and in what kind of group.
• He found that the park was busiest on Friday afternoons, mostly with families.
• He concluded that the park had become the district's main weekend meeting place.
questions.q: The student wants to describe the methods of Lotfy's study. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
c: Lotfy studied how residents of one district use a newly opened public park.
Lotfy concluded that the new park had become the district's main weekend meeting place.
The park Lotfy studied was busiest on Friday afternoons, mostly with families.
To learn how residents used the new park, Lotfy observed it for 120 hours over six months, recording who came, when, and in what kind of group.
questions.e: The goal is the method, so the sentence must say what Lotfy did to gather data: 120 hours of observation, recording who, when and in what groups. The other choices give the topic, a finding or the conclusion.
ce: It names the topic but not how he carried out the study.
This is the conclusion, not the method.
This is a finding, not the way the study was done.
Correct: it describes the method: how long he observed and what he recorded.

questions.p:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• The Aswan High Dam was built across the Nile in southern Egypt and completed in 1970.
• Its reservoir, Lake Nasser, is one of the largest artificial lakes in the world.
• The dam controls the Nile's yearly flood, protecting farms and towns downstream.
• It also produces hydroelectric power.
• However, the dam traps the silt that the flood once spread over farmland downstream, where it acted as a natural fertilizer.
questions.q: The student wants to present both a benefit and a drawback of the Aswan High Dam. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
c: Lake Nasser, the reservoir of the Aswan High Dam, is one of the largest artificial lakes in the world.
The Aswan High Dam controls the Nile's yearly flood and produces hydroelectric power.
Completed in 1970, the Aswan High Dam controls the Nile's yearly flood, but it also traps the silt that once fertilized farmland downstream.
The silt carried by the Nile's flood once acted as a natural fertilizer for farmland.
questions.e: The goal asks for a benefit and a drawback, so the sentence needs both flood control (or power) and the trapped silt; only one choice has both. The flood-and-power choice gives two benefits but no drawback.
ce: A fact about the reservoir, neither a benefit nor a drawback of the dam.
Two benefits and no drawback.
Correct: it gives one benefit (flood control) and one drawback (trapped silt) in a single sentence.
It hints at the drawback but never mentions the dam or a benefit.

questions.p:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• In stop-motion animation, figures are moved very slightly and photographed one frame at a time.
• When the photos are shown in quick succession, the figures appear to move on their own.
• Films are usually shown at 24 frames per second.
• A single second of stop-motion film can therefore require up to 24 separate photographs.
• One small studio's 80-minute stop-motion film took its team three years to complete.
questions.q: The student wants to emphasize how time-consuming stop-motion animation can be. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
c: Because a single second of stop-motion film can require up to 24 separate photographs, one studio's 80-minute film took its team three years to complete.
In stop-motion animation, figures are moved very slightly and photographed one frame at a time.
When the photos are shown in quick succession, stop-motion figures appear to move on their own.
Films are usually shown at 24 frames per second.
questions.e: To emphasize how time-consuming stop-motion is, the sentence should connect the many photos per second to the long production time; only one choice does. The technique choice is accurate but does not stress the time.
ce: Correct: it links the huge number of photos per second to the three years of work, which emphasizes how slow the process is.
It explains the technique but does not emphasize how long it takes.
It describes the effect on the viewer, not the time needed.
A general fact about films, with no link to the effort stop-motion requires.

blocks.title: After the test
items: **Read every explanation**, including those for questions you got right: check that you chose the answer for the right reason, not by luck. Each choice has its own short reason.

**List your weak skills.** Use your score by skill and write down every skill where you lost two or more questions, plus the trap that caught you (reversed, too extreme, half-right, off-topic, nearest-noun, comma splice…). The "Study these again" links take you straight to the lessons.

**Go back to the matching lessons:** Words in Context and High-Value Vocabulary for SAT Reading and Writing; Text Structure and Purpose; Cross-Text Connections; Central Ideas and Details; Command of Evidence: Textual; Command of Evidence: Quantitative; Inferences; Sentence Boundaries; Extra Information: Commas, Dashes and Brackets in Pairs; Semicolons; Colons; Subject–Verb Agreement; Pronoun–Antecedent Agreement; Verb Tense and Aspect; Verb Finiteness; Dangling and Misplaced Modifiers; Plurals and Possessives; Transitions; Rhetorical Synthesis (Student Notes).

**Redo every question you missed** after the lesson and its practice page, without looking at the explanation, and say aloud why each wrong choice is wrong. Then take Practice Test 9 under the same timed conditions.
**Check your timing.** If you did not finish a module, study Time Strategy and How to Attack Every Question before your next full test.
